questions.question: What is a webhook?

options.text: Server-initiated HTTP callback to a client-specified URL when an event occurs

questions.explanation: Webhooks are HTTP callbacks—when an event occurs, the server makes an HTTP POST to a URL you've registered. It's push-based: no polling needed. Common for payment notifications, CI/CD triggers, etc.

questions.question: Which scenarios are ideal for webhooks? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Payment gateway notifying your server of completed transactions
GitHub notifying your CI system of new commits
Stripe alerting your system of subscription changes

questions.explanation: Webhooks excel at event notifications between services: payments, CI triggers, subscription updates. Real-time gaming needs persistent low-latency connections (WebSockets), not HTTP callbacks.

questions.question: What security measure should webhook receivers implement?

options.text: Verify webhook signatures using shared secret

questions.explanation: Webhook endpoints are public URLs—anyone could send fake requests. Providers include signatures (HMAC) using a shared secret. Receivers must verify signatures to ensure requests are authentic.

questions.question: A webhook delivery fails (receiver returns 500 error). What should the sender do?
questions.explanation: Webhook senders should implement retry logic with exponential backoff (e.g., retry after 1min, 5min, 30min). This handles temporary failures while avoiding overwhelming struggling receivers.

questions.question: Why should webhook receivers respond quickly (within seconds)?

options.text: Senders have timeouts and may retry, causing duplicate deliveries

questions.explanation: Webhook senders timeout quickly (5-30 seconds typically). Slow responses trigger retries, causing duplicates. Best practice: acknowledge immediately (return 200), process asynchronously via queue.

questions.question: What is webhook idempotency and why is it important?

options.text: Handling duplicate deliveries without side effects

questions.explanation: Network issues and retries can cause duplicate webhook deliveries. Idempotent handling (using event IDs to detect duplicates) ensures processing the same webhook twice doesn't cause problems like double-charging.

questions.question: Which challenges exist with webhooks? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Webhooks require public endpoints (challenging for local dev), don't guarantee order (events may arrive out of sequence), and debugging is hard (you can't easily replay or inspect failed deliveries). They don't need persistent connections.

questions.question: How can developers test webhooks during local development?

options.text: Use tunneling services (ngrok) to expose local server
Deploy to production for each test

questions.explanation: Tunneling services like ngrok create public URLs that forward to localhost, enabling webhook testing during development. Many providers also offer webhook replay/testing tools in their dashboards.

questions.question: A payment provider sends webhooks for order updates. Your system receives 'order.completed' before 'order.created'. How should you handle this?

options.text: Store events and process in correct order using timestamps
Assume webhooks always arrive in order
Request the provider to fix ordering

questions.explanation: Webhook ordering isn't guaranteed. Robust systems store events with timestamps and either process in order or handle out-of-order gracefully (e.g., create order if it doesn't exist when completing).

questions.question: True or False: Webhooks provide guaranteed exactly-once delivery.
questions.explanation: Webhooks typically provide at-least-once delivery—retries ensure delivery but may cause duplicates. Exactly-once is extremely difficult over HTTP. Receivers must handle duplicates idempotently.

questions.question: What information should a well-designed webhook payload include? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Complete current state of the resource

questions.explanation: Good webhook payloads include: event ID (for idempotency), event type (for routing), timestamp (for ordering), and resource state (to avoid additional API calls). Some include only IDs, requiring receivers to fetch details.

questions.question: A webhook receiver is overwhelmed with traffic during a sale. What pattern helps manage this?

options.text: Reject all webhooks during high traffic

questions.explanation: Acknowledge webhooks immediately (return 200), push to a queue (SQS, RabbitMQ), and process asynchronously. This decouples receipt from processing, handling traffic spikes without losing events or triggering retries.
